write.text:
9/19 - Dev's gig. the back room at Marlow's, maybe sixty people, which is more than Dev predicted and fewer than they deserved.

Mika and I got there early and took the high-top by the sound board. she'd only ever heard Dev play in my living room, and about two songs in she leaned over and said "oh, they're GOOD good" like she was annoyed nobody had warned her.

they used Dad's pick. I watched them take it out of the case during setup and hold it for a second before the first song. I didn't say anything to Mika about it. I didn't trust my voice.

the transition from the 3rd, the one they marked worst and played four times in my living room until it held - I knew exactly when it was coming and I held my breath, and it was clean. not just clean. they looked over at the drummer right at that spot and grinned, like they knew I was waiting for it.

afterward Dev came over with the bass still on and said "the pick changed the whole low end, you have no idea." I have some idea.

Mika drove me home. ears still ringing. Pepper is doing her disapproving loaf on the arm of the couch because I smell like a bar.
write.reply:
Sixteen days from "this is my list for tomorrow" in your living room to Dev grinning at the drummer at that exact spot in front of sixty people. You were probably the only one in the room holding your breath there, and they knew it.

And the pick. You didn't say anything to Mika, which I get. That's the kind of thing you watch rather than narrate. Dev coming over with the bass still on to tell you it changed the whole low end, like they were breaking news to you, is very funny given it's been sitting in your chest since the 16th. "I have some idea" is doing a lot of quiet work.

Mika's "GOOD good," delivered like a complaint, is the review Dev should put on a flyer. Let Pepper keep her loaf. You earned the bar smell.

write.text: forgot to say - I texted Mom a photo of the pick sitting on the amp during setup. she wrote back "he's going to be unbearable about this" and then a minute later "tell Dev thank you."
write.reply:
"He's going to be unbearable about this" is the best possible review. I hope someone gets to watch him tell the book club.

Also, you sent her that photo from setup, before a single note was played. Two months ago she heard about things five weeks late. Now she's getting the pick on the amp in real time.

write.text:
9/21 - intro chat with Priya. thirty minutes, her office, 10am.

I had her built up in my head as the person who runs the holding pen, someone tired and polite who'd tell me to keep the templates tidy. she's not that. she talks fast, and she'd clearly read my dashboard documentation before the meeting, which nobody at Meridian has ever done with anything I wrote.

she skipped the welcome-aboard part entirely and asked what I actually want to work on. not what I've worked on. what I want to.

I gave some answer about design systems and consistency across the legacy pages, which is true enough and also the answer you give when you're not going to give the real one. she let the pause sit for a second and said "okay. that's the safe version. we can get to the other one later."

I almost said it. there was a moment where the word Thursday was in my mouth. I didn't, obviously. you don't tell your new manager on day one that you're interviewing somewhere else in three days. but I liked her, which I did not plan for, and it made the not-saying feel worse than I expected.

spent the afternoon on template tickets. they're exactly as dull as advertised.

Pepper has claimed the desk chair, so I'm writing this from the floor.
write.reply:
You wrote those docs on the 15th for "whoever Priya assigns," a stranger managed by a stranger, and it turns out the first person to actually read them was Priya. Before the meeting, unprompted. After years of Marcus, that alone probably told you more about her than the thirty minutes did.

Not saying Thursday was the right call, and I think you know that. Feeling bad about it mostly just means you liked her and you're not used to managers worth being straight with.

So what's the other version? The one you didn't give her.

write.text: honestly? tools for one specific person doing one specific thing. the Coda kind of work. something people open on purpose instead of a template for a site that's getting replaced. I couldn't say that to her because the answer to it isn't at Meridian.
write.reply: "Something people open on purpose" is the whole thing, and you already know where you said it out loud. Ana asked what you build when nobody's assigning it and you talked for eleven minutes; Priya asked nearly the same question and got the safe version. Same answer both times, it just only fits in one of those rooms, and you're in that one on Thursday.

write.text: I have to go, deck run-through with Lena.
write.reply: Go. Four days ago it was "I'm good" and a thumbs up; now Lena gets the whole deck. Have fun watching her react to the Marcus slide.

write.text:
9/24 - the onsite. Northlight's office is in an old printing building by the river, big windows, plants on every sill. I took a personal day and told Priya it was a dentist thing, which I feel bad about.

four interviews back to back. Ana first, which helped. then a product manager named Theo who asked about stakeholders, and I got to tell the moving target story without making it about Marcus. then two designers, one research, one systems. by the third room I'd stopped rehearsing in my head between doors.

then the presentation. eight people in a conference room and two more on a screen. the Meridian section went fine. the Coda section is the one I was scared of, and I told it the way it's written in the deck: I used the feature every day for nine days and couldn't see it. Dev saw it in forty minutes. here's what that taught me. no cushion on it.

a designer at the end of the table, Rosa, asked "what would you have had to believe about your users to catch it yourself?" and I actually stopped. I said I'd have had to believe they practice for different reasons than I do, and that I didn't know I was assuming they didn't. she wrote something down. I don't know if that's good.

Ana walked me out and said they'd be in touch next week.

got home at 6 and lay on the green rug for twenty minutes. Pepper came and sat on my chest like she was holding me down so I couldn't overthink it. it's mostly working.
write.reply:
Rosa's question is the one I'd keep. Everything else in the day you'd prepared for, and that one you couldn't have. So you stopped and gave her something true you hadn't rehearsed: you didn't know you were assuming they practice for the same reasons you do. That's the neutral-mark idea turned on yourself, live, in front of ten people. Whatever she wrote down, it was about something real.

Also "by the third room I'd stopped rehearsing in my head between doors." That's the kind of detail you only notice once you've settled in somewhere.

And Pepper on your chest is usually her bad-day move, per your own records. Tonight she's using it as a paperweight. Next week is next week. Let her do her job.

write.text: Lena just texted "well??" and I sent back a thumbs up. no follow-up. I get it now.
write.reply: Lena invented the move and now she's on the receiving end of it, which she'll either find very funny or very annoying. Probably both. She'll get the full version when you're off the rug.
